$comment: WHAT A PUBLISHED OPENAPI DOCUMENT MAY NEVER CARRY. One registry, two enforcers.
Read by ragcore/src/ragcore/api/openapi.py and by
dotnet/tests/Synthia.ContractTests/OpenApiEmissionTests.cs. Both stacks publish contracts, so
both apply the same list — two hand-maintained copies drift, and the drift is invisible until
the weaker of the two is the one that mattered.
IT LIVES IN A DATA FILE FOR A SECOND REASON. These terms are the shapes a credential takes, so
a list of them written as string literals in application source is indistinguishable, to a
secret scanner, from the credentials it is describing. tests/security/test_azure_identity.py
found exactly that and was right to: a policy list and a leaked key look the same from the
outside. Keeping the vocabulary as data rather than as code resolves it without weakening
either guard.
MATCHED AGAINST NAMES, NEVER DESCRIPTIONS. A document explaining that an operation carries no
credential is correct documentation; a field called apiKey is a defect whatever it holds today.
A scanner that flagged the prose would get the prose deleted, and then nobody remembers why.

secretTerms.$comment: Substring match against a normalised name. 'api_key', 'apiKey' and 'api-key' all reduce to 'apikey'.

$comment: Exact match against a normalised name, not substring: 'roles' must not be a parameter, but a
schema called 'AcceptedRolesSummary' is a legitimate read model and a substring rule would
reject it.
Two different things are in this list. The first group is implementation detail — a client
that can see it starts depending on it, and then the detail is a contract nobody agreed to.
The second group is authority the platform DERIVES and never accepts: publishing a parameter
named for one advertises exactly what the platform refuses, and a client that sent it would
get a silent no-op rather than an error, which is the worst of both.

structuralKeys.$comment: Keys of the OpenAPI format itself, skipped. 'security' and 'securitySchemes' describe HOW to authenticate and never with what.
